QF.id: Introduction to AML, CFT and Proliferation Financing_12

question.text: The Palermo Convention (2000) expanded AML efforts beyond drug trafficking by:

answer.text: Extending the criminalization of money laundering to proceeds from ALL serious crimes, not just drug trafficking
Creating the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) as a permanent intergovernmental body
Establishing the Egmont Group of Financial Intelligence Units
Requiring all countries to set up dedicated Financial Intelligence Units

explanation.text: The Logic: The UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, commonly known as the Palermo Convention (2000), expanded the global AML approach beyond drug trafficking by requiring state parties to criminalize the laundering of proceeds from a broad range of serious crimes. This built on the earlier Vienna Convention (1988), which had been narrower in scope. The Trap: FATF was established by the G7 in 1989, before Palermo, and not by the Convention itself. The Egmont Group of FIUs was a separate informal initiative for FIU cooperation, also not created by Palermo. Requiring all countries to set up FIUs is more directly traceable to FATF Recommendations and domestic legislation rather than to the Palermo Convention. Note: The specific Palermo Convention framing, including the "extends criminalization to proceeds from all serious crimes" wording, was not found in the cited NISM Series XXIV workbook pages, which reference the Vienna Convention but not Palermo. The framing above reflects general international AML-history knowledge rather than a direct workbook citation.
